> JSON.stringify formats it as
> JSON.stringify(new Date())
> '"2022-09-04T22:38:07.082Z"'
> and ClickHouse does not like this format.

`JSON.stringify` accepts a function to customize the output. See [replacer](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/JSON/stringify#the_replacer_parameter). It suffices to reformat Date to a compatible string.
Cons: It adds overhead to traverse the object before serialization.
```js
JSON.stringify(obj, (key, value) => {
  if(value instanceof Date) return formatDateToString(value)
```

Hi @slvrtrn!

I'm willing to work on adding support for nested data types.

My approach would be to flatten the nested structures, such as objects. So, I would choose the `Record<K, V>` TS type to support the `Nested` data type, because both have the same goal, to handle structured data.

If we assume the explanation, then we face incompatibility with the `Map(K, V)` data type. According to the **[official docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/integrations/language-clients/nodejs#supported-clickhouse-data-types)**, the `Map(K, V)` data type is supported by the `Record<K, V>` TS type.

This means that I won’t be able to differentiate between `Map` and `Nested` when attempting to flatten them.

In my opinion, the `Map(K, V)` data type should be supported by the `Map<K, V>` TS type. There are a couple of advantages to supporting it as a TS Map:

- It would create semantic coherence between the Clickhouse data type and the TS type.
- The TS Map API is better suited for handling data map structures than the TS Record type.

What do you think about supporting Clickhouse Map with TS Map?

Many thanks

Hi @antoniovizuete, thanks for your interest in the project.

IIRC, JS Maps introduction will likely require additional decoding effort when working with JSON* types. Right now, it just does `JSON.stringify/parse` (see the [source](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/7a8f0d18908c00f9b45e9e28a6514b1eff8df349/src/data_formatter/formatter.ts#L66-L100)), but with JS Maps, we will likely need to replace it with a better codec. I guess we just wanted to keep it as simple as possible.

Another question, for datasets with large maps, do we expect significant serialization/deserialization performance difference between the current implementation (plain objects) and JS Maps?

As for Nested, I don't think the problem is in the `Record<K, V>` type that we use; for tests, I could not figure out a proper way to insert records with `Nested` - again, IIRC, the inserted rows had empty columns no matter what without the actual Nested object.

Does it behave the same if you follow [this endless JSON stream example](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/main/examples/endless_flowing_stream_json.ts#L35-L52)?

That's the exact scenario we tested for the streaming of large inserts continuously for prolonged amounts of time.

Please note that we don't await the insert promise here. The chunks of the data are periodically dumped into the stream, and it is never closed until we hit Ctrl+C. Then, finally, we finalize the stream and await the promise.

Thanks for pointing it out.

The reason why we added these additional typings is that you could provide these settings on a query basis ([for example](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/97a61622b5d979f2326061845735d1d01472ad04/__tests__/integration/clickhouse_settings.test.ts#L21-L24)), so it is better to have some types there for development experience in the IDE.

I appreciate the commentary on the inserts. For my particular case it is not important that the latency between the `push` into the stream event and the eventual appearance in the table be optimized. As long as that latency is reasonably fast (order minutes) it would be fine. My reading of the comments is that an amount of data less than `max_insert_block_size` could be buffered indefinitely until the stream is actually closed. This means, for me, during busy times it is not necessary to close / reconnect the stream, but when things slow down, a close / reconnect will guarantee the latency is never more than a threshold I can code to. So that works for me. 

If you have any ideas on how to control memory when inserts are happening very quickly, I'd like to hear about them.

We must have been reading the same stuff. I was trying to `push(null)` and allocate a new stream when there was back pressure but couldn't get that to work. I'll give your solution a go!

I noticed you resend the row when there is back pressure. This is not necessary. The indication of back pressure (return of `false`) does not indicate a failure to do the insert, just that the buffers are reaching thresholds. You can see that resending duplicates rows by running the query:

```
    select count(*) as nRow, count(distinct id) as nId 
    from default.test_ch_conn
```

and you'll see nId < nRow.

I think I need to add handling of the drain event to adjust properly for the back pressure. Looking into that now and will post here the finished result.

Nice catch! 

EDIT: yeah, the `drain` event handler could've been more robust in this case, as we possibly can improve the performance by avoiding any "sleeps". However, the "sleep" might be handy as we can fine-tune the delay if the application does something other than data ingestion.

EDIT2: wrapping every insert in a Promise has a huge negative performance impact, though. So, in the end, `drain` seems like the best solution.

It turns out the `Readable` stream does not emit drain events when back pressure has eased. I ended up with a solution that keeps the client open, but creates a new stream every few seconds to push the inserts into. I found a long lived stream led to memory issues and/or excessive delivery delays (as mentioned in the comments above). 

With the new arrangement things are so far looking good, so I'm closing this.

Currently, we are considering several scenarios to move forward with the client, preferably with as little breaking change as possible, for example:

1. Replace the connection layer with a one-size-fits-all implementation (suitable for Node.js and Browser/etc with polyfills) that at least will not use a built-in Node.js HTTP module. That implementation could be based on, for example, fetch or axios. But, for instance, `node-fetch` has its own problems on the Node.js platform (https://github.com/node-fetch/node-fetch/issues/1735, https://github.com/node-fetch/node-fetch/issues/1588, etc). However, it's unclear (or, more precisely, I haven't investigated it yet) how to support features such as mutual TLS in this scenario, as it uses https.Agent currently.

2. Extract the current Node.js-specific connection layer into a separate package (and call it something like `@clickhouse/client-node-connection`) and require the Connection class to be passed when the client instance is created. This way, it will be possible for the users to implement a custom Connection that could work in their runtime. 

^ All of the above covers usage of the `http` and `zlib` modules. As for the `streams` module, I think we could adjust it to use https://www.npmjs.com/package/web-streams-polyfill in the client based on the availability in the current runtime.

Personally, I am more in favor of the second option with a customizable Connection.

Please let me know what you think.

I think I finally found where the problem here is (it's a nasty one, though).
And it is especially noticeable when you are using only one connection. 

What is happening here is that we have an incoming response stream for insert/exec, which is not consumed in the code, and that stream is holding the socket for as long as `request_timeout` allows. Then, the socket quietly times out (which is an issue on its own cause it's not logged properly), and the program continues as normal cause everything is fine - we received 200 OK, it's just the stream that was eventually destroyed.

However, likely, it will introduce a bit of a breaking change in `exec` - we need to understand whether we want to ignore the incoming stream and destroy it ASAP, releasing the socket, or we want to consume it in the code.

Additionally, it looks like this is also related to #150, and that's also caused by the underlying sockets timeout.

@movy, I agree that the KeepAlive topic is rather confusing, especially in Node.js with all the different timeouts and lack of proper socket housekeeping out of the box, etc.

Can you please share a snippet of your code that was derived from the endless stream example? Node.js/OS versions will also help.

I am curious how a hang-up error can happen when basically one connection is open indefinitely.

But the fact that `keep_alive: {enabled: false}` did not help as well is rather surprising. 

Usually, what happens is:
- With KeepAlive enabled, there is a pool of open sockets that HTTP Agent "manages".
- Since there is no reliable way to terminate idle sockets out of the box (even `agentkeepalive` library with `freeSocketTimeout` setting does not help), they are still considered "usable" even if the server has already closed the connection on its side
- when such an "expired" socket is assigned from the pool to a new request, and we try to send something, we have `socket hang up` cause the remote side is shut down.
- without KeepAlive, the sockets should be connected/reconnected every time we create a new request, so it should theoretically bypass the problem entirely at a cost of some performance.
 
But I do not expect this to be happening _without_ KeepAlive enabled.

Additionally, can you please confirm that this:

```ts
const client = createClient({
  keep_alive: {
    enabled: true,
    socket_ttl: 2500, // less than the server's KeepAlive timeout
    retry_on_expired_socket: true,

})
```

By design, `query` and `exec` will hold the socket until the stream is either consumed or destroyed - otherwise, there is no way to stream the data; `await query(...)` will essentially await only the response as if it was successful or not, the actual data is incoming only after iterating over the stream or calling `json` and `text`, both of which will consume the stream under the hood.

It is designed in such a way cause we want to be able to stream an arbitrary amount of data without running into OOM issues. This is also why we don't implement any buffering in advance.

`command` and `insert` will release the sockets immediately as we do not expect anything useful there in the response.

I wanted to post an update here, as this issue looks stale while it is not.

I've been studying RowBinary format and writing an experimental implementation of it with select streaming support out of the box for quite some time already; current progress is here: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/compare/1.0.0...row_binary

At the moment of writing this, that branch supports _decoding_ a minimal set of useful data types:

* Boolean 
* (U)Int8/16/32 as a `number`
* Float32/64 as a `number`
* (U)Int64/128/256 as a [native JS BigInt](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/BigInt)
* String
* Date/Date32 as a JS Date.
* Nullable

Currently in progress, as I consider the following types should be supported straight away (there are drafts decoders/placeholders for some already): Decimal, Enum, UUID, FixedString, DateTime(64), Array, Map, Tuple.

NB: under the hood, [Date is just a UInt16](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/sql-reference/data-types/date) (number of days since Unix Epoch), and [Date32 is just an Int32](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/sql-reference/data-types/date32) (also days, but before/after). JS Date is chosen only as _the default_ option for these types; there will be a mapping option to convert the "days" numeric value to any other object.

For example, consider the Date type. The mapper is just:

```ts
<T>(daysSinceEpoch: number) => T
```

And, by default, if no custom mapper is provided, it is something like this:

```ts
const defaultDateMapper = (daysSinceEpoch: number) => new Date(daysSinceEpoch * DayMillis)
```

Similarly, Date32, DateTime, DateTime64 (especially DateTime(9) as it requires proper nanoseconds support), and Decimal will have optional mappers support from their decoded "raw" representation.

It supports streaming of the following JSON family formats (see the `EachRow` in the format name except [JSONObjectEachRow](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#jsonobjecteachrow)):

* [JSONEachRow](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#jsoneachrow) <- easiest to use.
* JSONStringsEachRow
* JSONCompactEachRow
* JSONCompactStringsEachRow
* JSONCompactEachRowWithNames
* JSONCompactEachRowWithNamesAndTypes
* JSONCompactStringsEachRowWithNames
* JSONCompactStringsEachRowWithNamesAndTypes

"Raw" formats can be streamed in and out, too:

* CSV
* CSVWithNames
* CSVWithNamesAndTypes
* TabSeparated
* TabSeparatedRaw
* TabSeparatedWithNames
* TabSeparatedWithNamesAndTypes
* CustomSeparated
* CustomSeparatedWithNames
* CustomSeparatedWithNamesAndTypes
* Parquet

I checked the doc entry: https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/integrations/language-clients/javascript#insert-streaming-in-nodejs - I understand now why this could be unclear.

 "JSON format" in the doc means [ClickHouse JSON Format, which is a single object](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#json) (NOT to be confused with JSON itself). 

The following ClickHouse formats could not be streamed (see the returned object shape [here](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats)):

 * [JSON](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#json)
 * [JSONStrings](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#jsonstrings)
 * [JSONCompact](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#jsoncompact)
 * [JSONCompactStrings](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#jsoncompactstrings)
 * [JSONColumnsWithMetadata](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#jsoncolumnsmonoblock)
 * [JSONObjectEachRow](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/formats#jsonobjecteachrow)

Thanks for raising this issue; the doc needs to be updated for clarity (plus add a few more "non-streamable" formats there).

There is [an example](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/main/examples/node/insert_file_stream_ndjson.ts) using NDJSON file and JSONCompactEachRow format.

If you want to use a regular JSONEachRow with a stream, which just accepts "normal" full serialized objects, then it's something like this:

```ts
// Assuming we read a few objects from somewhere.
function getStream() {
  const stream = new Stream.Readable({
    objectMode: true, // required for JSON* family formats
    read() {
      //
    },
  })
  
  stream.push({ id: 42, name: 'foo' })
  stream.push({ id: 144, name: 'bar' })
  stream.push(null) // this closes the stream
  return stream
}

const stream = getStream()
await client
  .insert({
    table: tableName,
    values: stream,
    format: 'JSONEachRow',
  })

// check that the table has 2 records now
const rs = await client.query({
  query: `SELECT * from ${tableName}`,
  format: 'JSONEachRow',
})
console.log(await rs.json())
```

```
➜  ~ curl -u "foo:bar:""" --data-binary "SELECT 1" "http://localhost:8123"
Code: 516. DB::Exception: foo: Authentication failed: password is incorrect, or there is no user with such name. (AUTHENTICATION_FAILED) (version 24.3.1.2672 (official build))
➜  ~ curl -u ""foo:bar":" --data-binary "SELECT 1" "http://localhost:8123"
Code: 516. DB::Exception: foo: Authentication failed: password is incorrect, or there is no user with such name. (AUTHENTICATION_FAILED) (version 24.3.1.2672 (official build))
```

NB: clickhouse-client uses TCP/Native, which, unlike the HTTP interface, does not send the username + password as the basic auth header, which is separated by a colon (and this is causing this issue).

NB2: JS URL is not happy about this, too:
```ts
new URL('http://foo:bar:qaz@localhost:8123/').username
'foo'
new URL('http://foo\:bar:qaz@localhost:8123/').username
'foo'
new URL('http://foo\\:bar:qaz@localhost:8123/').username
''
new URL('http://foo%3Abar:qaz@localhost:8123/').username
'foo%3Abar'
new URL('http://"foo:bar":qaz@localhost:8123/').username
'%22foo'
new URL('http://\'foo:bar\':qaz@localhost:8123/').username
'%27foo'
new URL('http://\"foo:bar\":qaz@localhost:8123/').username
'%22foo'
```

This: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/pull/253/files#diff-46e9eda9880b41c04095d911536817d628992924b2bdd3a96f66529dd3628a5bL101-L104

Unless JIT optimizes it out (it does not), it's at least one extra full pass, worst case two.

The web auth spec is pretty clear: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2617#section-2

```
user-pass   = userid ":" password
userid      = *<TEXT excluding ":">
password    = *TEXT
```

Even if we fix it by sending different headers on the connection level (and adjust a fair bit of tests accordingly), it will still not work with an upcoming [URL configuration](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/392bd82fdc1c0ffa82332c033e40bd05a5c71707/CHANGELOG.md#url-configuration), and it will require different hacks there (and more testing), as it is essentially working with the JS URL object (which behaves differently than cURL, which still does not work).

I'd say that, for now, we won't fix it. Please use a username compatible with HTTP auth standards.

I'll ask our admin to make the change to the username to exclude `:`.

Meanwhile, where can I file an feature request for `clickhouse-client` to add validation to disallow `:`-containing usernames? Or does that require a deeper change to the SQL interpreter?

We could only do that if the username is provided via the configuration object.

However, this use case (with URL configuration) is tricky:

```
> const u = new URL('http://foo:bar:qaz@localhost:8123/db')
> u.username
'foo'
> u.password
'bar%3Aqaz'
```

Currently, it does not look like we can reasonably assume anything in the client config parser. Multiple colons by the HTTP auth standard are disambiguated with all colons going into the password part, as it is allowed only there. As you can see in the example above, it _always_ goes into the password part (with an automatic URI component encoding), effectively cutting off the rest of the username, which we think was intended to be `foo:bar` (but we have no way to validate that with the URL, as it could've been username `foo` + password `bar:qaz`, and it is perfectly valid).

If you know a workaround for the HTTPS Agent on the Bun platform, you could try providing a custom agent like it is described here: https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/integrations/language-clients/javascript#custom-httphttps-agent-experimental-nodejs-only (see the "Using a custom HTTPS Agent with mutual TLS" part in particular), but if it's simply not used, that won't help either.

e.g. 

```ts
const client = createClient({
  application: 'MyApp'
})
```

will result in the `User-Agent` header like the following:

The problematic part in your code is this:

```ts
  const [result1, result2] = await Promise.all([
    client.query({ query }),
    client.query({ query }),
  ]);

  const [json1, json2] = await Promise.all([result1.json(), result2.json()]);
```

What happens: having only one connection available, with this

```ts
  const [result1, result2] = await Promise.all([
    client.query({ query }),
    client.query({ query }),
  ]);
```

Without consuming the result set immediately, the first query will hold the socket until it is closed by ClickHouse, which is regulated by that keep_alive_timeout server setting; only then will the second query be executed after the first one timed out, as a new socket becomes available in the internal connection pool. 

As the query is only `SELECT 1`, the entire data is sent immediately with the response, so it doesn't fail explicitly.

The correct approach is to run query + process the result set as soon as it is available, for example:

```ts
async function queryRun(client: NodeClickHouseClient, query: string) {
  const resultSet = await client.query({ query })
  return resultSet.json() // <- fetch the data immediately!
}

async function batchRun(client: NodeClickHouseClient, index: number) {
  const _query = `SELECT 1`

  const start = Date.now()
  const [json1, json2] = await Promise.all([
    queryRun(client, _query),
    queryRun(client, _query),
  ])

  const elapsed = Date.now() - start
  console.log(
    `Run ${index + 1} took: ${elapsed}ms (${json1.rows},${json2.rows})s`,
  )
}

async function main() {
  const client = createClient({
    max_open_connections: 1,
  })

  for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    await batchRun(client, i)
  }
}
```

In this case, everything works as expected:

```
Run 1 took: 12ms (1,1)s // <- this is a tad bit slower as it isn't KeepAlive yet
Run 2 took: 3ms (1,1)s
Run 3 took: 3ms (1,1)s
Run 4 took: 3ms (1,1)s
Run 5 took: 3ms (1,1)s
Run 6 took: 3ms (1,1)s
Run 7 took: 3ms (1,1)s
Run 8 took: 3ms (1,1)s
Run 9 took: 2ms (1,1)s
Run 10 took: 2ms (1,1)s
```

Side note: in your example, the main does not fail only because the query is `SELECT 1`, which yields the entire response data immediately; replacing the query with something like `SELECT * FROM system.numbers LIMIT 1000`, especially with a reduced `request_timeout` setting will illustrate that the socket just times out

```
        at Socket.emit (node:domain:488:12)
        at TCP.<anonymous> (node:net:337:12)
```

Regarding ResultSet consumption on the application side, there are a few mentions in the client docs on the website about this, see https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/integrations/javascript#query-method and https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/integrations/javascript#resultset-and-row-abstractions in particular.

The client does not add these CAST calls by itself; sending the query such as in your example:

```ts
const rs = await client.query({
  query: `
    SELECT number FROM base WHERE number = ({ n: Int32 })
  `,
  format: 'JSONEachRow',
  query_params: {
    n: 456,
  },
})
```

This will be a rough equivalent of the following cURL:

```
curl "http://localhost:8123?param_n=456" \
  --data-binary "SELECT number FROM base WHERE number = ({ n: Int32 }) FORMAT JSONEachRow"
```

The actual query processing/translation is up to the server (and in the server logs, you probably see the fully rendered query with that added `_CAST`); the client does not modify the original query except for adding the FORMAT clause and sending the rest of it as-is.

See also: https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/interfaces/http#cli-queries-with-parameters.

Here are the answers from the team regarding the `_CAST` operation itself:

- The literal 456 in the query is interpreted as `UInt16` while the parameter has type `UInt64`.
- The casting is done in all cases to accommodate this in a general way.
- `_CAST` is a constant expression, which is free (zero cost).

I don't think we can simply use `constants` because previously, when the "max string length" value was unbound, it was throwing a cryptic error that was difficult for the end user to understand, and that happened even on a 64-bit system: see https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/pull/357; that's why it is limited to exactly that value.

Hello @slvrtrn, thank you for the answer.

The [introduced variable](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/4affe3432b99c5189ec8fa0cd9f7d6923d812d66/packages/client-node/src/utils/stream.ts#L4) into `clickhouse-js` equals to `536870888` and it works perfectly with 64-bit architectures. Unfortunately, this value is higher than the 32-bit architecture supports in terms of the v8 engine. V8 engine value for 32-bit is [268435440](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/3a3130dfd68ed2945d94328bbefea626190d1f1d/include/v8-primitive.h#L127C46-L127C60). It means that we can't catch issue by [this condition](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/main/packages/client-node/src/utils/stream.ts#L16) when the codebase is running into 32-bit. 

I have checked node versions from 16 (because package.json says this library supports only ^16), and all major node versions have the `MAX_STRING_LENGTH` variable equal to `536870888`.

The changes in this PR haven't changed the flow of the function, and it should catch this error as before. However, using variables from `node` helps us catch the issue for both use cases, not only for 64-bit.

We don't support batching queries on the client side. Multi-statements are not supported on the server side.

```bash
curl "http://localhost:8123" \
  --data-binary "SELECT 42; SELECT 144;"
```

```
Code: 62. DB::Exception: Syntax error (Multi-statements are not allowed): failed at position 10 (end of query): ; SELECT 144;. . (SYNTAX_ERROR) (version 25.2.2.39 (official build))
```

Similarly, it cannot be used in the CLI client. There is a [multiline option](https://clickhouse.com/docs/interfaces/cli#command-line-options-query), but it will split the queries and send them separately anyway.

So, even if we parse the specified queries, or receive them as an array, we will have to use separate connections/sockets for them anyway, essentially running a similar `Promise.all`, but internally.

Sure, I had some code that was chaining insert calls like this:
```
this.promise = this.promise.then(() => insertPromise).catch();
```

Using catch without any parameters actually throws the error instead of swallowing it 🤕  (see [here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/catch#description))

I fixed this by using
```
.catch(error => { this.failed.push(error); });
```
and handling those errors through additional logic elsewhere.

The last resort is overriding the header limit in the runtime itself via e.g. `--max-http-header-size=32768`

I think what happens here is that an implicit conversion occurs only in queries with the VALUES clause.

Consider this example from the CLI client:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE foo
(
    `i` UInt128
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO foo VALUES (generateUUIDv4());

SELECT *
FROM foo;
```

This works and prints:

```
   ┌───────────────────────────────────────i─┐
1. │ 239166372890801806463433812033336270121 │ -- 239.17 undecillion
   └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

However, see what happens with cURL (and this client, consequently, as it works in a similar way):


```sh
echo -ne '{"i":"018b81cd-aca1-4e9c-9e56-a84a074dc1a8"}' | \
  curl 'http://localhost:8123/?query=INSERT%20INTO%20foo%20FORMAT%20JSONEachRow' \
  --data-binary @-
```

This fails similarly to your report, since it does not convert the values implicitly:

```
Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected '"' before: 'b81cd-aca1-4e9c-9e56-a84a074dc1a8"}': (while reading the value of key i): (at row 1)
: While executing ParallelParsingBlockInputFormat. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) (version 25.6.2.5 (official build))
```

Perhaps you could convert the UUID in the app and then pass BigInt as a str? 

Alternatively, [EPHEMERAL columns](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/create/table#ephemeral) should work.

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE foo
(
    `i` UInt128 DEFAULT j,
    `j` UUID EPHEMERAL
)
ENGINE = Memory
```

An example with cURL:

```sh
echo -ne '{"j":"018b81cd-aca1-4e9c-9e56-a84a074dc1a8"}' | \
  curl 'http://localhost:8123/?query=INSERT%20INTO%20foo%20(j)%20FORMAT%20JSONEachRow' \
  --data-binary @- 
```

```sh
clickhouse-client --query "SELECT * FROM foo"                                                                                                                  

2053589985159873382859980112667722152
```

See the TS example: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/blob/main/examples/insert_ephemeral_columns.ts

Hey! I ran into the same issue when performing `INSERT` operations using `@clickhouse/client`.

In my case, the error disappeared after removing the following settings from the `createClient` call:

- `async_insert_max_data_size`
- `async_insert_stale_timeout_ms`

Keeping only `async_insert` and `wait_for_async_insert` seems to work consistently.

```diff
    client = createClient({
      url: `http://${host}:${port}`,
      username,
      password,
      database,
      clickhouse_settings: {
        async_insert: 1,
        wait_for_async_insert: 0,
-      async_insert_max_data_size: "30MB",
-      async_insert_stale_timeout_ms: 100,
      },
    });
```


Hope it helps anyone facing this issue.

So, in other words, we haven't left anything important behind. ## AI analysis Here's a comparison of your pre-Vitest and post-Vitest coverage reports: ### Overall Coverage Changes | Metric | Pre-Vitest | Post-Vitest | Change | |--------|------------|-------------|--------| | Statements | 96.44% | 95.52% | **-0.92%** | | Branch | 87.94% | 91.31% | **+3.37%** | | Functions | 98.01% | 96.98% | **-1.03%** | | Lines | 96.52% | 95.63% | **-0.89%** | ### Key Observations **Improvements:** - **Branch coverage increased significantly** (+3.37%), indicating better testing of conditional logic paths - Several files achieved 100% branch coverage that previously didn't: - `client.ts`, `settings.ts`, `format_query_settings.ts`, `json_handling.ts` - `connection.ts`, `sleep.ts`, `stream.ts` (in utils) - `compression.ts`, `create_connection.ts`, `node_http_connection.ts` - `config.ts`, `runtime.ts`, `user_agent.ts` **Regressions:** - Statement and function coverage decreased slightly (under 1%) - **`process.ts` coverage dropped dramatically**: from 66.66% to 0% (statements and lines) - `client.ts` in client-node/src dropped from 85.71% to 50% statement coverage - `formatter.ts` branch coverage decreased from 75% to 66.66% ### Files Needing Attention 1. **client-node/src/utils/process.ts** - Complete loss of coverage (0%) 2. **client-node/src/client.ts** - Significant statement coverage drop 3. **client-common/src/parse/column_types.ts** - Still has 10 uncovered lines in both reports 4. **client-node/src/connection/node_base_connection.ts** - Increased uncovered lines (from 8 to 12) The migration to Vitest improved branch coverage meaningfully but lost some statement/function coverage, likely due to test setup differences or tests that weren't properly migrated. **Pattern:** All 8 missing files are **`index.ts`** files - these are typically barrel export files that re-export other modules. This explains some of the coverage drop. These files likely aren't being included in the Vitest coverage collection, possibly due to: - Different coverage configuration (e.g., excluded patterns) - How Vitest handles re-exports vs the previous test runner - Missing `include` patterns in the Vitest config You should check your Vitest coverage configuration to ensure barrel files/index files are being included.

Current workaround on our side (until there is guidance/fix upstream):

- For these `JSONEachRow` reads, we switched from `client.query(...).json()` to `client.exec(...)`.
- We append `FORMAT JSONEachRow` in SQL and parse newline-delimited JSON directly from the returned stream.
- This avoids the `ResultSet.json() -> ResultSet.stream()` guard path that can throw `"Stream has been already consumed"` in this scenario.

This is working reliably for us, but we would prefer the standard `query(...).json()` path if there is a recommended way to avoid this race.

## Code Review Summary

I've completed a comprehensive review of the PR changes. Here's my analysis:

### ✅ **Strengths**

1. **Robust Implementation**: The feature correctly tracks `freed_at_timestamp_ms` on sockets and uses timestamp-based checks to detect stale connections independently of timer accuracy (socket_pool.ts:430-431, 499-526).

2. **Well-Guarded Edge Cases**: The eager destroy logic is properly gated behind `keep_alive.enabled && keep_alive.idle_socket_ttl > 0` (socket_pool.ts:104-107), preventing the issue where `idle_socket_ttl = 0` would destroy every free socket.

3. **Safe Iteration**: The eager-destroy loop correctly iterates over a shallow copy of the socket array (`[...byHostSockets]`) to avoid mutations during iteration (socket_pool.ts:113).

4. **Backwards Compatible**: All new parameters are optional with sensible defaults (`eagerly_destroy_stale_sockets?: boolean` defaults to `false`), maintaining backwards compatibility.

5. **Comprehensive Testing**: The integration tests in `node_eager_socket_destroy.test.ts` cover both the eager-destroy path and the stale-reuse warning path with stable baseline timestamps and proper async handling.

6. **Clear Documentation**: The CHANGELOG entry provides a clear explanation and usage example.

### 🔍 **Observations**

1. **Test Reliability**: The tests use a 50ms sleep to ensure sockets return to `freeSockets` before the second request (lines 69, 145). The recent commit (dc277d2) added a 1000ms grace period for the stale-reuse warning threshold, which should improve reliability in CI environments.

2. **Log Message Quality**: The WARN log correctly references `keep_alive.eagerly_destroy_stale_sockets` (socket_pool.ts:513), matching the user-facing configuration path.

3. **Test Independence**: The tests use a custom HTTP server (`createHTTPServer`) and `createTestClient` which, despite the name, can be configured to point to the local server rather than requiring ClickHouse. The tests pass the `url` parameter explicitly (line 45, 122), making them effectively independent of the ClickHouse test environment.

### 📊 **Architecture Assessment**

The implementation follows a clean separation of concerns:
- Configuration (config.ts:34-38) → Connection factory (create_connection.ts:32) → Base connection (node_base_connection.ts:46) → Socket pool (socket_pool.ts:104-150)

The feature integrates naturally into the existing socket lifecycle management without introducing breaking changes or architectural debt.

### ✅ **Verdict**

The changes are production-ready. All previous review feedback has been addressed correctly, and the implementation demonstrates solid understanding of Node.js socket lifecycle, event loop timing issues, and edge cases in concurrent systems.

I've looked at the PR more closely again. What makes me a bit hesitant to right away merge this IMO important feature:
* we're changing semantics a bit which I'm not sure we're ready to invest in testing
* we'd need to support exceptions that are in-bound in the HTTP/1

I'd like to be able to give away a really raw unfiltered stream and give an option for the consumer to bolt on the exception detection as a stream transformer. This might require some refactoring and documentation.

Having said this, the exception detection can wait, we can always just expose the raw response stream and document that it's ATM not supporting dealing with in-bound exceptions.

WDYT?

Thanks for the response, @peter-leonov-ch !

I agree on both points. The _consumed flag refactor (638e020) was mostly a response to Copilot's review comments and isn't strictly necessary - the original `readableEnded` check was fine for the existing methods. I'm happy to revert that commit to keep the PR scoped to the new feature only.

For the in-band exceptions, that's new to me, but I think the pragmatic path is to document that rawStream() does not handle them, and defer exception detection to a follow-up, maybe even mark them as rawStreamUnsafe (but I mean, raw is.. raw). We can always add an optional transform later without breaking the API.

So the plan would be:
- Revert 638e020  
- Add a note to the rawStream() docstring that in-band ClickHouse exceptions are not detected
- Keep everything else as-is

Is that right?

The `run-examples (head, node)` job failed in `cancel_query.ts` with a socket timeout on `KILL QUERY ... wait_end_of_query=1`. Reproducing locally against `latest` ClickHouse passes — the failure only happens against ClickHouse `head` because the published `@clickhouse/client@1.18.3` doesn't yet contain the fix that's currently in this repo (unreleased `1.18.4`). In e04b8ea I dropped `head` from the `run-examples` matrix so this job validates the published client against released ClickHouse (which is what end users actually run). Compatibility of the in-tree source with ClickHouse `head` is still covered by the integration test jobs.

> @copilot debug the CI error. It runs ok locally, but fails in CI.

Debugged it: the failing CI job logs show `long_running_queries_cancel_request.ts` exiting with code 1 at line 63 — the `if (!insertQueryExists)` branch. That's the `pollOnInterval('CheckQueryExists', …, { intervalMs: 100, maxPolls: 50 })` (5 s budget) timing out before the QueryStart entry shows up in `system.query_log`.

Locally with no contention the entry appears within ~300 ms (Poll #3/4), but in CI all ~50 example processes share one ClickHouse via Vitest `pool: 'forks'`, so flush latency on the shared `query_log` exceeds 5 s. The fix in c4d1d87 bumps `maxPolls` for the existence check to 200 (20 s headroom, still well under the 60 s vitest test timeout) — `flush_interval_milliseconds=1000` is configured in `.docker/clickhouse/single_node/config.xml`, so this is purely about absorbing CI fork contention. The `CheckCompletedQuery` step is unchanged.

From our production case, a warning would not be enough for real double-consumption. We use these results in analytics/usage/reporting paths, where silently continuing after a second consumer could turn into empty or partial data and hide a real application bug.

The issue for us was specifically treating stream lifecycle state as consumption state. Fast `JSONEachRow` responses can have `readableEnded === true` before the first user-level `json()` call, while buffered data is still available. Our workaround was to avoid `query(...).json()` for these reads and use `exec()` + `FORMAT JSONEachRow`, then drain and parse newline-delimited JSON ourselves.

So our preferred behavior is:

- first `json()`/`text()`/`stream()` call should be allowed even if the underlying stream has already ended but has not been consumed by the ResultSet API;
- later consumption attempts should still throw deterministically;
- the guard should be based on an explicit ResultSet-level consumed flag, not `readableEnded`.

In short: yes, a ResultSet-level guard is useful, but warning-only would be risky for our use case.

@copilot check if the published types with the new strict rules might affect end users of this library

> @copilot check if the published types with the new strict rules might affect end users of this library

Checked. The new strict compiler flags themselves do not propagate to consumers; only the emitted `.d.ts` shapes matter. Most public-surface changes are `foo?: T` -> `foo?: T | undefined`, which is generally more permissive for consumers (especially with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`) and should not break runtime behavior. The main possible TS-only impact is stricter narrowing in consumer code that relied on property-presence checks (`'foo' in obj`) to imply non-`undefined`; such sites may need an extra `undefined` check.

### Benchmark findings: use `undici.request()`, not `fetch()`

Updated this benchmark to compare against **`undici.request()`** instead of the global `fetch()` — and it materially changes the conclusion.

The earlier `fetch()`-based stub lost the **download** scenario by ~5×, which initially read as "http/https is much faster at streaming large results". That gap turned out to be entirely the **WebStreams (`ReadableStream`) response-body layer** that `fetch()` routes through — a known Node-core bottleneck ([nodejs/undici#1203](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/issues/1203)) — not a property of the undici transport. `undici.request()` returns a native Node `Readable` (the same stream type `@clickhouse/client` drains), which is the API a real migration would actually adopt.

Indicative local run (macOS/Apple Silicon, Node v24.6.0, ClickHouse `head`, loopback, default config), stable across two runs:

| Scenario | `@clickhouse/client` (http/https) | `undici.request()` stub |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SELECT 1` latency (mean) | ~2.1–2.7 ms | ~0.50 ms (~4–5× faster) |
| Download throughput | ~1310–1440 MiB/s | ~1850–1920 MiB/s (~1.3–1.4× faster) |
| Upload throughput | ~223–225 MiB/s | ~241–245 MiB/s (~tied, server-bound) |

With native streams, `undici` (low-level API) is faster or tied across the board — supporting the "or better yet with undici directly" framing in #511. Caveats unchanged: this is a bare transport stub vs the full client (omits settings/retries/compression/keep-alive tuning/abort/logging), and loopback numbers will overstate the gaps vs a remote/cloud endpoint. Re-run per workload.

Thanks @bobdevries — you're right that overloading one field with `boolean | string` isn't the cleanest design; a codec-only field would be tidier on its own merits.

For me it comes down to the trade-off against backward compatibility. `compression: { request?: boolean }` / `{ response?: boolean }` is the current public API, so going codec-only would break every existing `request: true` / `response: true` caller and force a config change on upgrade. For an established, widely-used option that felt like a steep price for the type-purity gain, so I leaned toward widening the existing type (keeping `true` = gzip) rather than replacing it.

Thanks for submitting an issue!

While I'm analyzing a more foundational response, let's start with a quick question. Did you try replacing the parameters with that script already? If yes, which corner cases have you noticed that a proper solution would cover better?

## Analysis

I recently looked at the query processing pipeline.

It has a rather cheap step where it only works with syntax: `EXPLAIN AST` ([docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/explain#explain-ast)). It does minimum but the result is likely now what you're looking for:

```bash
curl -v 'http://localhost:8123/?param_a=5&param_b=5' --data-binary 'EXPLAIN AST SELECT {a:UInt8} = {b:String}'
```

returns:

```yaml
SelectWithUnionQuery (children 1)
 ExpressionList (children 1)
  SelectQuery (children 1)
   ExpressionList (children 1)
    Function equals (children 1)
     ExpressionList (children 2)
      Function _CAST (children 1)
       ExpressionList (children 2)
        Literal UInt64_5
        Literal \'UInt8\'
      Literal \'5\'
```

And there is also `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` ([docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/explain#explain-syntax)) that does more than just parsing (it expands names, deals with some function expansion) and returns the full query with parameters interpolated (thanks @chernser for the hint!):

```bash
curl -v 'http://localhost:8123/?param_a=5&param_b=5' --data-binary 'EXPLAIN SYNTAX SELECT {a:UInt8} = {b:String}'
```

returns:

```SQL
SELECT _CAST(5, \'UInt8\') = \'5\'
```

This might be what can tick most of the boxes.

And there is just `EXPLAIN` that does a [lot more](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/explain#explain-plan).

## Suggestion

All of the above require another request to the server and some extra processing on the server side. If this is appropriate, the `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` might be the most robust option as it does not introduce any new moving parts.

There is also an option with `system.query_log` but on a cluster it might require some extra coordination to get to the right log.

> query insights

This is a good start to understand if full queries with params are what you really need, but as a robust sollution, no doubt, it's not feasible.

Did you check the `system.opentelemetry_span_log`? The docs on [Open Telemetry](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/opentelemetry) support in CH look promising.

And there is always an option to parse the actual query using the alpha SQL parser: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js-parser and interpolate the parameters manually, but parsing in JS normally produces a lot of of temporary objects and strings and might create a visible pressure on GC.

Let me know which path you'd like to explore more.

I also implemented the per-codec request options as we agreed over Slack: the public `request` option is a discriminated union, so each codec carries its own knob — `level` for gzip/zstd, `quality` for brotli:

```ts
request?:
  | boolean
  | { codec: "gzip"; level?: number }
  | { codec: "zstd"; level?: number }
  | { codec: "br";   quality?: number }
```

It's backward-compatible with the gzip/zstd `{ codec, level }` form, and `createRequestCompressor` now takes the `RequestCompression` object so each codec's option flows through (and future codecs whose switch isn't a numeric `level` fit cleanly).

`br` is wired for both request and response. Unlike zstd it has no minimum Node.js version (zlib has had brotli since 11.7), so there's no availability guard; for inserts it defaults to quality 4, since zlib's brotli default of 11 is far too slow for a streaming body.

## Security review — OSS-dependent integration tests

Reviewed the CI workflow, the vitest config changes, and all 22 ingested test files. **Bottom line: low risk, and notably well-handled.**

The most reassuring finding: despite the "ingested third-party code" framing, none of these files contain pasted upstream source. Each is a hand-written ~70–150 line *reproduction* that mirrors how the dependent uses the client — readable, auditable, no opaque blobs, no vendored code, no transitive-dep or license surprises.

### Checked and clean

- **No egress / no dynamic execution.** Across all 22 files there's zero network activity beyond the local test ClickHouse. The only non-client imports are `node:stream` and a `node:http` Agent (posthog). No `eval`, `child_process`, `fs`, `fetch`, or dynamic `require`. Every client is built via the repo's own `createTestClient()` → localhost. The two literal external URLs (`https://example.com` in firecrawl) are String *column values*, never fetched.
- **No secrets / credentials.** Nothing reads env for credentials or exfiltrates anything; all connection params come from the test helper.
- **CI workflow is properly hardened** — the part that usually goes wrong when running PR-supplied code is done right:
  - `permissions: {}` — the `GITHUB_TOKEN` has no scopes.
  - Triggered by `pull_request`, **not** `pull_request_target` — fork code never runs in a privileged, secret-bearing context. This is the single most important control and it's correct.
  - All third-party actions pinned to full commit SHAs.
  - No `secrets.*` referenced anywhere; the blast radius of any malicious PR is just the ephemeral runner.
- **SQL handling models good practice.** Dynamic values use server-side parameterization (`{indicator:String}`, `{table:Identifier}`, …). Table names are interpolated but from `guid()` (repo-generated UUIDs), not external input — not an injection vector.

### Minor notes (not vulnerabilities)

1. **~~`npm install` → `npm ci`~~** — addressed: CI now uses `npm ci` for reproducible, lockfile-pinned installs.
2. **The tests faithfully reproduce "run arbitrary SQL" surfaces** (arkime's analyst-configured query, tooljet's `run(query)`, growthbook's raw SQL). That accurately reflects how those *upstream apps* work — it's not something this PR introduces. Fine in a test; just be aware these examples aren't demonstrating a locked-down query API.

No security action required.

**CI note — the failing `code-quality` (Prettier) check is pre-existing, unrelated to this PR, and non-blocking.**

The single failing check is the whole-tree `prettier --check .` step in `code-quality`, and it flags exactly one file:

```
[warn] CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
[warn] Code style issues found in the above file. Run Prettier with --write to fix.
```

That file is **not part of this PR's diff** — it is byte-identical to `main`. All five files this PR actually changes (`packages/client-common/src/client.ts`, `packages/client-node/CHANGELOG.md`, `packages/client-web/CHANGELOG.md`, and the two new test files) are Prettier-clean.

Root cause: `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` was added to `main` in #942 in a state Prettier reformats. The `node` workflow (`.github/workflows/tests-node.yml`, which hosts the whole-tree `code-quality` job) only triggers on changes under `packages/**`, `tests/**`, `package.json`, etc. — root-level markdown is excluded from both its `push` and `pull_request` path filters. So the whole-tree formatting gate never ran on #942, and it doesn't run on `main` pushes for that file either. This PR is the first `packages/**` PR after #942, so it is simply the first to run `prettier --check .` against the unformatted file.

Since `code-quality` is not a required status check, this PR is already mergeable (`mergeStateStatus: UNSTABLE`, not `BLOCKED`), and the insert-columns backtick-quoting fix is complete — all functional checks (unit, integration, cluster, cloud) are green.

I've intentionally kept the `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` reformat **out of this bug PR** to keep it to a single concern. It's best fixed at source on `main` (`npx prettier --write CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`), which would also unblock the whole-tree gate for every future `packages/**` PR; I've flagged that as a separate follow-up.

### Re-confirmation before fixing: the `%2E` output does not reproduce over HTTP — `@clickhouse/client` is working as intended here

I tried to reproduce this against running servers before writing a fix, and the reported behavior does not occur on the HTTP interface that `@clickhouse/client` / `@clickhouse/client-web` use. Details below so this is a self-contained record.

**Environment**
- `clickhouse-js` `main` @ `0f8458b`
- ClickHouse servers: **25.9.7.56** (same 25.9 line the source bug referenced) and **26.5.1.882**
- HTTP interface (port 8123) — the transport this client uses

**What the setting actually does**
```
name:        json_type_escape_dots_in_keys
value:       0
default:     0
description: When enabled, dots in JSON keys will be escaped during parsing.
```
It governs how a `.` inside a JSON key is treated **when the document is parsed on insert**: `=1` → the dot is a literal character of the key; `=0` (default) → the dot is a nested-path separator.

**Exact repro from the issue (setting = 1 on all queries), over HTTP:**
```sql
CREATE TABLE test_json (data JSON) ENGINE = Memory;
-- INSERT INTO test_json FORMAT JSONEachRow {"data": {"a.b": 123, "c": {"d.e": 456}}}
SELECT * FROM test_json FORMAT JSONEachRow;
```
Server HTTP output — **identical on 25.9.7.56 and 26.5.1.882**:
```json
{"data":{"a.b":123,"c":{"d.e":456}}}
```
`FORMAT JSON` is likewise correct (`meta.type = "JSON"`, `"a.b": 123`, `"d.e": 456`). So `JSON.parse` on the response body yields `{"a.b":123,"c":{"d.e":456}}` — the dots are already dots. The `Actual: {"a%2Eb":123,...}` in the report does **not** happen over HTTP when the setting is on.

The only way to see `%2E` over HTTP is to **read with the setting off** (`json_type_escape_dots_in_keys=0`) data that was inserted with it on:
```json
{"data":{"a%2Eb":123,"c":{"d%2Ee":456}}}
```
That is the documented raw/stored form, deliberately selected by the reader's setting — the client is faithfully relaying it, not mangling anything.

**Why the `clickhouse-connect` fix (#572) does not translate to this client**
connect's fix lives in the **native binary protocol** reader (`datatypes/dynamic.py::_read_column_binary`). Over the native protocol a `JSON` column arrives as a flat list of **dotted typed-path strings**, and the client reconstructs the object with `split('.')`; to keep a literal-dot key distinct from the path separator, such keys are escaped as `%2E` **inside the path names**, so connect had to `unquote` each segment. `@clickhouse/client` is **HTTP-only** and consumes **server-formatted JSON text** — the path reconstruction and dot (un)escaping are done server-side, so there is nothing for the client to post-process.

**A blanket client-side `%2E`→`.` unescape would be a regression, not a fix.** Percent sequences are legitimate data elsewhere; e.g. over HTTP:
```sql
SELECT map('x%2Ey', 5) AS m FORMAT JSONEachRow;  -- {"m":{"x%2Ey":5}}
SELECT 'lit%2Eval'      AS s FORMAT JSONEachRow;  -- {"s":"lit%2Eval"}
```
Both must round-trip verbatim. And the streamable `JSONEachRow` family (which the report cites) carries **no per-column type metadata** — only `FORMAT JSON`/`JSONCompact` include a `meta` block — so the "scoped to JSON-typed columns" step the report asks for isn't even expressible in that pipeline. `json_handling.ts` / `JSON.parse` is therefore the correct, minimal behavior.

**Conclusion:** there is no defect in the `json_handling.ts` / `JSON.parse` path described here. With `json_type_escape_dots_in_keys=1`, `@clickhouse/client` already returns the original dotted keys.

One pointer for maintainers, **separate from this HTTP path**: the `@clickhouse/rowbinary` reader returns a `JSON` column as a `Map` keyed by the flat dotted path (`skills/clickhouse-js-node-rowbinary/src/readers/json.ts`), which is the same binary-protocol representation connect operates on. If any client-side fidelity gap exists in clickhouse-js it would be there, not in the HTTP `JSON.parse` path — but that is a different code path (and a different package) than this issue reports, and would need its own reproduction to confirm.

Closing as **not a bug**, per the validation above.

To summarize: with `json_type_escape_dots_in_keys=1`, the HTTP interface already returns the original dotted keys (`{"data":{"a.b":123,"c":{"d.e":456}}}`) on both 25.9.7.56 and 26.5.1.882, so `@clickhouse/client` / `@clickhouse/client-web` return them correctly today — there is nothing to fix in `json_handling.ts`. The `%2E` form only appears when reading with the setting turned off, which is the documented raw/stored representation. The `clickhouse-connect` counterpart (#572) applied to that client's **native binary** typed-path reconstruction, which this HTTP-only client does not perform.

If a fidelity gap is ever found in the `@clickhouse/rowbinary` reader (`src/readers/json.ts`), which is the one place this repo handles the binary typed-path form, that would warrant a separate issue with its own reproduction.

Closing this — withdrawing the change, and correcting the record on my own PR description.

The description claimed that because `union` is one of git's **built-in** merge drivers it needs no setup and therefore "works for every contributor, for CI, and for merges performed on GitHub." **That last part is wrong.** GitHub does not honour `.gitattributes` merge drivers — including the built-in `union` — in any of its server-side git operations:

- the **Merge / Squash / Rebase** buttons
- the **"Update branch"** button
- mergeability and conflict detection (*"This branch has conflicts that must be resolved"*)
- the web conflict editor

Those all use GitHub's own merge implementation, which ignores merge drivers entirely. So two PRs each adding a changelog entry would **still** be reported as conflicting on github.com and would still need a manual resolution there. The attribute would only ever take effect when a contributor merges or rebases locally in their own clone — a small fraction of the benefit this PR was proposed for, and arguably a downside on its own, since in that path it resolves silently with no conflict for anyone to review.

The rationale that justified committing this file therefore doesn't hold, so I'd rather close it than leave a misleading claim in the tree. Sorry for the noise, and thanks for the review time.

@peter-leonov-ch Thanks, you are right. The detector looked only at the current chunk. ClickHouse writes the exception block (up to 16 KiB) at the end of the response, but the client can receive it split across chunks.

I reproduced this against a live 26.9 server (2 KiB to 15 KiB messages, no compression). In 2 of 16 runs the block was split. The previous head then emitted `\r`, `__exception__\r`, and `<tag>\r` as rows, followed by a wrong error message.

Pushed aa33dcf (Node and Web):

- Detection now uses the block **opening** `\r\n__exception__\r\n<tag>`, also when the opening is split across chunks. If a chunk ends before it is possible to decide, the bytes from the start of that row are kept and scanned again with the next chunk. This applies only after a `\r\n`, so JSON formats are not delayed.
- From the opening on, the block is buffered until its closing `<tag>\r\n__exception__\r\n` arrives (capped at the server's 16 KiB), then parsed. Block bytes are never emitted as rows.
- At the end of the response, an incomplete block is an error.
- New tests split the response at every byte, and deliver it one byte at a time, for LF and CRLF rows. They also cover a 16 KiB block in 4 KiB chunks and successful CRLF/binary bodies. These tests fail on the previous head and pass now.
- Against the live server: 48 of 48 runs now give the real error and 0 block rows.

Hi @Mohil-Ahuja, apologies it's taken so long to respond.

Thanks for opening the PR, this is a clear improvement. I checked the change against a live ClickHouse server (`head` image) and it fixes the #973 cases. Details below, plus two inputs where the same error still happens.

### How I tested

For each of 44 queries, I compared the server's answer to two requests:

- the original query, sent unchanged with `?default_format=JSONEachRow`, so the server applies the format without the client changing the text;
- what `query()` sends: `removeTrailingSemi(query.trim()) + " \nFORMAT JSONEachRow"`.

The queries were the #973 examples, every input from this PR's unit tests, and 16 extra edge cases.

| | Same answer as the server |
|---|---|
| `main` | 25 / 44 |
| this PR | 42 / 44 |

The PR is never worse than `main` on these 44 queries, and every input from its own tests works against the real server. Nested `/* */` comments, `#!` comments, `\r` line endings, doubled quotes inside backtick names, and Unicode-quoted names (`“a;”`) all work too.

### Two inputs that still fail with `Multi-statements are not allowed`

**1. `$` inside an identifier**

```sql
SELECT 1 AS a$t$; -- $t$
```

ClickHouse allows `$` in bare identifiers, and only starts a heredoc at a `$` that begins a token. The scanner checks for a heredoc at every `$`, so `$t$; -- $t$` is read as a heredoc and the real `;` is never found. A possible fix is to only check for a heredoc when the previous character can't be part of a word:

```ts
if (c === "$" && (i === 0 || !/[A-Za-z0-9_$]/.test(query.charAt(i - 1)))) {
```

**2. `//` line comments**

```sql
SELECT 1; // note
```

The server accepts `//` as a line comment (the query above returns `1` when sent as-is), but the scanner only recognises `--` and `#`. Adding `(c === "/" && next === "/")` to the line-comment branch should fix it.

Both also fail on `main`, so they aren't regressions. Could you add them to `remove_trailing_semi.test.ts` along with the fixes?

```ts
["SELECT 1 AS a$t$; -- $t$", "SELECT 1 AS a$t$ -- $t$"],
["SELECT 1; // note", "SELECT 1 // note"],
```

### Changelog

The entries were added under the `1.24.0` heading. 1.24.0 and 1.24.1 have been released since this branch was created, so after rebasing on `main` they need to move to the next unreleased heading.

Thanks @Mohil-Ahuja, that was quick! I re-ran the same checks on 5776b67.

### Results

- **Server-judged comparison:** the same 44 queries now get the same answer as the server for **44 / 44** (42 / 44 before). Both cases from my last comment are fixed.

### Performance: an easy fast path

`removeTrailingSemi` now runs a full scan on every `query()`, `command()` and `exec()` call. That's negligible for normal queries, but it adds up for large ones. On `main` the check is effectively free (Node.js 22, median of 5 runs):

| Query | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| typical `SELECT` (~850 B) | ~0 ms | 0.01–0.06 ms |
| 2 MB `INSERT … VALUES` | ~0 ms | 16–56 ms, depending on the data |

A query without any `;` has nothing to remove, so the scan can be skipped:

```ts
export function removeTrailingSemi(query: string): string {
  if (!query.includes(";")) {
    return query;
  }
  // ...
```

It makes the 2 MB `INSERT` without `;` go from about 18 ms to 0.03 ms. Queries that do contain a `;` keep the current cost.

#1085 (closing #1079) changes `query()` to send the SQL as written and pass the format as the `default_format` setting, so the client no longer edits the query text. That removes most of the reason for this issue:

- **#973** (`SELECT 1; -- note`) and **#970** (`FORMAT` after a trailing `SETTINGS`) were both caused by the appended `FORMAT`. With nothing appended, they are fixed for everyone, with no opt-in and no extra package. The short `SHOW ROW POLICIES` case (#759) is fixed the same way.
- **Trailing semicolons:** `command()` and `exec()` also send the SQL as written now. The only remaining client-side edit is `exec()` with `values`, where the server needs the statement to end without a `;` before the data. That is a plain end-of-string trim that doesn't need a lexer.
- So `sql_lexer`, the rewriter and the `FORMAT`/`SETTINGS` placement (steps 1-6 of the rollout, #1065-#1070) would have nothing left to do. The same goes for the hand-written scanners in #1031 and #972.

What may still be worth doing, separately from this issue:

- Using `@clickhouse/lexer` in this repo's tests, e.g. for the SQL scanning in `tests/clickhouse-test-runner` (`split-queries.ts`, `backends/rowbinary.ts`).
- Safer identifier quoting in `insert()` (#945, #1004), if that still needs SQL-aware handling.

Suggest closing this issue and the draft PRs once #1085 merges. If the test-runner or `insert()` ideas are worth keeping, they can go into new, smaller issues.

I tried the request #1085 sends (the query as written plus `default_format=<format>`) against what `main` sends (`<query> FORMAT <format>`) on a 26.10.2.103 server, over plain HTTP so only the server behaviour was compared.

**Same results as `main`:**

- `SHOW TABLES ... LIKE`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXISTS`, `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, `EXPLAIN`, `WITH ... SELECT`, `UNION ALL`, `SHOW PROCESSLIST`, `SHOW SETTINGS` and `... SETTINGS max_threads=1` all return the same rows in the requested format.
- `SELECT 1; -- note` now returns JSON. On `main` the appended `FORMAT` lands inside the comment, so the server answers in TSV.
- Users with `readonly=1` and `readonly=2` profiles can still query. `default_format` is accepted from them, so sending it on every request doesn't lock out read-only users.
- Errors are byte-for-byte the same apart from the echoed query text, with the same HTTP status (400 syntax, 404 unknown table, 500 `throwIf` before output). The mid-stream `__exception__` block with its tag is also unchanged, for JSON, JSONEachRow and CSV. So `parseError` and the exception-tag handling need no changes.

**One suggestion: the format the server actually used is in the response.** The new failure mode is a `FORMAT` clause left in a `query()` call: it used to fail with a syntax error and now quietly changes the output format, so the result set fails later on a parse error. The server reports the format it used in `X-ClickHouse-Format`:

| request | `X-ClickHouse-Format` |
|---|---|
| `default_format=JSON`, `SELECT 1` | `JSON` |
| `default_format=JSON`, `SELECT 1 FORMAT CSV` | `CSV` |
| `default_format=JSON`, `SELECT 1 FORMAT JSONEachRow` | `JSONEachRow` |
| `default_format=JSON`, `CREATE TABLE ...` / `INSERT ... VALUES` | (absent) |

So `query()` could compare the header with `format` when it is present and throw a clear error, for example "the query has a FORMAT CSV clause, but format is JSON". That brings the early failure back, and statements with no output are unaffected. Happy to open a follow-up for it after this merges if that's useful.

## About the red `upstream-sql-tests` check

The 16 failing `upstream-sql-tests` jobs are the only failing checks on this PR, and **this release doesn't cause them**. We'll fix them on `main` after 1.25.0 ships.

**Cause.** The workflow runs ClickHouse's own SQL test suite against the `latest` server image. The test suite is pinned to a June 2026 ClickHouse commit. On 2026-10-25, `latest` moved from 26.9 to 26.10, and 16 tests began failing because the server output no longer matched the old expected results (for example, the byte layout of serialized aggregate states). `main` has failed this way every night since. The same commit, `e829009`, passed on 10-24 (server 26.9.19.9) and failed on 10-25 (server 26.10.2.103).

**Checked against the last release.** With the test suite pinned to 26.10, the same 9 tests fail on `release`, which is the 1.24.1 code ([run](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41446398353)), and on `main`, which is 1.25.0 ([run](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41445264743)). No test fails only on `main`.

### Fixes coming after the release

A follow-up PR to `main` from `test/upstream-sql-tests-26.10`, already passing all 20 jobs in [this run](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-js/actions/runs/41451523273):

- Pin the upstream test suite to `v26.10.2.103-stable`, to match the `latest` server.
- Close three gaps where the test runner, our stand-in for `clickhouse-client`, behaved differently from the real client:
  - It treated `--port` as an HTTP port. In the real client, `--port` is the native TCP port, and since the newer test-suite version the runner passes `--port=9000` to shell-script tests.
  - It read `-n` as `--multiline` instead of `--multiquery`, and it didn't run every statement passed with `-q`.
  - In rowbinary mode it printed Decimals with trailing zeros, which the server's text output drops.
- Comment out two tests that need server config our Docker image doesn't have: `03707_autopr_unsupported_cases` (a `parallel_replicas` cluster) and `04103_plain_rewritable_get_last_modified_bug` (`custom_local_disks_base_directory`).

### A client bug this found

`02515_generate_ulid` exposes a bug in `parseError` that is already in released versions. It isn't a regression, and 1.24.1 fails the same way. The server repeats the failing query inside its error message, and the regex takes the first all-caps word in parentheses as the error type. So for a query containing `materialize(NULL)`, the error gets `type: 'NULL'` instead of `TOO_MANY_ARGUMENTS_FOR_FUNCTION`, and the message is cut short at the same point. It affects both clients. The follow-up PR comments the test out with a pointer to this bug, and the fix will come in a separate PR with changelog entries for `@clickhouse/client` and `@clickhouse/client-web`.

None of this has been reported in an issue or PR yet. I checked; the only related item, #1096 / #1097 (heredoc splitting in the test runner), covers different tests.

A reproduction of defect 2 on `@clickhouse/client` 1.25.0, with the trailer a real server sends. No proxy is involved: the hang only needs a TCP read that ends right after the trailer's opening `\r\n`.

ClickHouse 26.8.36.3 ends the body of `SELECT number, throwIf(number = 50000) FROM numbers(1000000) FORMAT JSONCompactEachRow` like this:

```
[49999, 0]\n\r\n__exception__\r\nlclegawbpaxkcrjg\r\nCode: 395. DB::Exception: ...\n289 lclegawbpaxkcrjg\r\n__exception__\r\n
```

When a chunk ends with `<row>\n\r\n` and carries no earlier `\n` (it holds the tail of a single row) and is longer than `1 + 13 + 2 + 16 + 2 = 34` bytes, the result set's transform finds the `\r\n`, calls `extractErrorAtTheEndOfChunk`, and the `do { --errMsgLenStartIdx } while (chunk[errMsgLenStartIdx] !== NEWLINE)` scan runs below index 0 without end. The whole process stops answering.

The script below (Node 24, `npm i @clickhouse/client@1.25.0`) serves that response from a local HTTP server, either in one write or split after the opening `\r\n`, and reads it in a worker so the main thread can report the hang.

<details><summary>repro.cjs</summary>

```js
const http = require('node:http');
const { Worker, isMainThread, workerData, parentPort } = require('node:worker_threads');

const TAG = 'lclegawbpaxkcrjg';
const MESSAGE = "Code: 395. DB::Exception: Value passed to 'throwIf' function is non-zero. (FUNCTION_THROW_IF_VALUE_IS_NON_ZERO)";
const TRAILER = `\r\n__exception__\r\n${TAG}\r\n${MESSAGE}\n${Buffer.byteLength(MESSAGE) + 1} ${TAG}\r\n__exception__\r\n`;

if (isMainThread) {
  const server = http.createServer((request, response) => {
    request.resume();
    response.writeHead(200, {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json; charset=UTF-8',
      'X-ClickHouse-Format': 'JSONCompactEachRow',
      'X-ClickHouse-Exception-Tag': TAG,
    });
    const row = `["${'x'.repeat(60)}"]\n`;
    if (process.argv[2] === 'whole') {
      response.end(row + TRAILER);
      return;
    }
    // First chunk: one row longer than the trailer's fixed tail, then the trailer's opening CR LF.
    response.write(row + TRAILER.slice(0, 2));
    setTimeout(() => response.end(TRAILER.slice(2)), 100);
  });
  server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', () => {
    const worker = new Worker(__filename, { workerData: { port: server.address().port } });
    const watchdog = setTimeout(() => {
      console.log('client event loop still blocked after 5 s');
      worker.terminate().then(() => server.close());
    }, 5000);
    worker.on('message', (outcome) => {
      clearTimeout(watchdog);
      console.log(outcome);
      server.close();
    });
  });
} else {
  const { createClient } = require('@clickhouse/client');
  const client = createClient({ url: `http://127.0.0.1:${workerData.port}` });
  (async () => {
    try {
      const resultSet = await client.query({ query: 'SELECT 1', format: 'JSONCompactEachRow' });
      for await (const rows of resultSet.stream()) {
        rows.forEach((row) => row.json());
      }
      parentPort.postMessage('no error');
    } catch (error) {
      parentPort.postMessage(`rejected: ${error.message}`);
    }
  })();
}
```

</details>

```
$ node repro.cjs whole
rejected: Value passed to 'throwIf' function is non-zero.
$ node repro.cjs split
client event loop still blocked after 5 s
```

The floor on the scan in #975 removes the hang. Reporting the server's own message for a split trailer is the cross-chunk part (defect 3 here, #1084 and #1086).

Until a release carries the floor, we fail the query ourselves as soon as a chunk holds a raw `\r`, before the client parses it. That is safe for the JSON formats, which escape control characters inside values, but not for binary or CRLF formats.

Adding one more reason for this change: abort handling. Both clients now need custom code to handle `abort_signal`, and that code has bugs.

## Related issues and PRs

- #1047 (Node.js): an `abort_signal` that is already aborted before the call is ignored. The wrapper in `getAbortController()` only listens for future `abort` events. The PR adds a check of `signal.aborted`.
- #1117 / #1118 (Web): the same bug in the Web client. `WebConnection.request()` sets `abort_signal.onabort = ...`, and an already-aborted signal never calls it. The PR adds an early check.
- Not fixed by #1118: the Web client assigns `onabort` instead of calling `addEventListener`. This replaces any `onabort` handler the user set. If two requests use the same signal, only the last request is aborted.

The two PRs fix the symptoms. The root cause is that each client builds its own abort logic around a second `AbortController`.

## The "proper" fix

The platform solves this already. `fetch()` (and also undici `request()`) accepts an `AbortSignal`. It rejects a pre-aborted signal without sending the request, and it also aborts the response body when the signal aborts later. `AbortSignal.any()` combines signals.

**Node.js:** move from `http`/`https` to `fetch()` (or undici). Then `getAbortController()` and the listener code are not necessary.

**Web:** the client already uses `fetch()`, but it wraps it. Replace the wrapper with:

```ts
const timeoutController = new AbortController();
const timeout = setTimeout(
  () => timeoutController.abort(),
  this.params.request_timeout,
);
const signal = params?.abort_signal
  ? AbortSignal.any([params.abort_signal, timeoutController.signal])
  : timeoutController.signal;
// fetch(url, { ..., signal }); clearTimeout(timeout) when headers arrive
```

This removes the `onabort` assignment and the `isAborted` flag. Keep the early `aborted` check, because users can pass a custom `fetch` that does not obey a pre-aborted signal.

## What custom code stays, and why

Two decisions about the current API keep some custom code:

1. **`request_timeout` stops when the response headers arrive.** A long streamed result can run longer than the timeout. `AbortSignal.timeout()` cannot be stopped and would cut long streams. So we need a timer that we can clear. To remove it, `request_timeout` must cover the full request, or users must pass `AbortSignal.timeout()` themselves.
2. **Error mapping.** The clients change the native `AbortError` into their own errors (for example `Error("The user aborted a request.")` in Web). Without this mapping, users get the standard `DOMException` (`name === "AbortError"` / `"TimeoutError"`) and the signal's `reason`.

Both are breaking changes. If we make them, we should make them together with the Node.js move to `fetch()`, so that both clients act the same.

About performance (see the comment above about the cost of `fetch()`): the abort argument is the same for `fetch()` and for undici `request()`. Both accept `signal`, so either choice removes this custom code.

## Also for v2: an `exports` field in `@clickhouse/client`

From the review of #1128. This is another breaking change of the package shape, so it fits into the same release.

### Problem

`@clickhouse/client` has no `exports` field. So native ESM cannot import a subpath without its full file name. The optional undici entry point shows this:

| Import | CommonJS, TypeScript, bundlers | Native ESM (`.mjs`, no bundler) |
|---|---|---|
| `@clickhouse/client/undici` | works | `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT` |
| `@clickhouse/client/undici/index.js` | works | works |

#1128 uses the longer path for native ESM as a workaround.

### Proposal

Add an `exports` field, for example:

```json
"exports": {
  ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" },
  "./undici": { "types": "./dist/undici/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/undici/index.js" },
  "./package.json": "./package.json"
}
```

Then native ESM accepts `@clickhouse/client/undici`, and the `undici/` folder stub can go away.

### Why this is breaking

With an `exports` field, Node.js and TypeScript (`node16`/`nodenext`/`bundler`) resolve only the listed paths. I tested a packed package:

| Deep import | Without `exports` (today) | With `exports` and a `"./*": "./*"` wildcard |
|---|---|---|
| `@clickhouse/client/dist/index.js` | works | works |
| `@clickhouse/client/dist/index` (no extension) | works | **`Cannot find module`** |

Deep imports without an extension are used in practice:
- langfuse imports `@clickhouse/client/dist/config` (see `packages/client-node/__tests__/oss-dependents/langfuse.test.ts`).
- Our own e2e test imports `@clickhouse/client/dist/version` (`tests/e2e/install/src/index.ts`).

So the v2 change should:
- export the types that users get from `dist/` today (for example `NodeClickHouseClientConfigOptions`) from the package root, so that they do not need deep imports;
- decide whether to keep a `dist/*` pattern for a transition period;
- list the removed deep imports in the migration notes.

The packed-tarball smoke test (`.scripts/smoke_test_pack.sh`, which now also runs in the `dist` workflow) checks the ESM and CommonJS imports. It can check the new `exports` field.

I reproduced it with `request_timeout: 1000`. With undici, every unread result crashed the process (`query()` and `exec()`, with an empty or a small body). With `node:http` there was no crash, and the next query worked.

The cause:
- For a small result, undici receives the complete response at once. The connection is then free, but the timer kept running.
- When it fired, it destroyed the body with an error. Nobody listened for that error, so it was an uncaught exception.

The fix:
- The timer stops when undici pushes the end of the body. A complete response holds no connection, so there is nothing to free. This is the same as `node:http`.
- When the timer fires and nobody listens for errors, it destroys the body without an error. The request is still aborted, and the connection is still released, but there is no uncaught exception.

After the fix, both transports give the same result in all 8 cases: no crash, and the next query works. The earlier stuck-pool cases still give the same results as before: an unread streaming result frees its connection after about 1 s, and an abort of a queued request rejects at once.
